analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for workers' menopause symptoms at work.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced in July 2026; none has acted, and it has 7 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more employees to make reasonable accommodations for workers whose menopause symptoms make parts of their job harder, unless the employer can show the accommodation would cause significant difficulty or expense. Simple accommodations like keeping water at a workstation, extra restroom breaks, or the option to sit or stand would be presumed reasonable without a doctor's note. It also covers federal, congressional, and state employees, directs the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to write rules within a year, and includes protections against retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits: Women experiencing menopause or the menopausal transition, a stage the bill notes can bring hot flashes, sleep disruption, and other symptoms for four to eight years. The bill's findings note that women ages 45 to 64 make up more than 17 percent of the U.S. labor force, and that menopause carries stigma that keeps many workers from asking for accommodations.

how_it_helps.text: Covered employers must provide reasonable accommodations to known menopause-related limitations of qualified employees unless doing so would cause an undue hardship, and cannot deny opportunities or force unpaid leave when another accommodation would work.

A list of simple modifications, including keeping water nearby, extra restroom breaks, and the option to sit or stand as needed, is presumed reasonable without requiring documentation from the employee.
It is unlawful to retaliate against a worker for requesting or using an accommodation, and information about an employee's condition must be kept as a confidential medical record.
Protections extend beyond private employers to congressional employees, federal employees, and state employees covered by existing civil rights employment statutes.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees bear the cost of providing accommodations and adjusting schedules or workstations; taxpayers fund a $4.5 million appropriation for the EEOC to write the required regulations. Employers below the 15-employee threshold are exempt.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers must engage in an individualized accommodation process and face damages and attorney's fees under the same enforcement framework as Title VII, which creates compliance and litigation exposure across any workplace with 15 or more employees.

The bill directs that terms like 'menopause, menopausal transition, symptoms and related effects' be construed broadly in favor of expansive coverage, and says courts should not demand extensive documentation of coverage, which business-side critics of similar laws argue creates uncertainty about what qualifies.

An employer that made good-faith efforts to accommodate can escape money damages on accommodation claims, but the bill still lets workers seek injunctive relief and fees, so disagreements over what counts as good faith are likely to end up in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accommodations required are mostly modest and inexpensive, and the bill mirrors the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act's structure, which set a precedent for this kind of protection. The main honest cost is compliance friction and some litigation risk for employers, and the definitional breadth means some coverage questions will be fought out case by case. For a large share of the female workforce, the practical value of not having to choose between health and a paycheck during a years-long transition is significant.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to four House committees on the same day in July 2026, and with no committee action since, it sits waiting while the session runs toward its January 2027 end.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 14, 2026, by Rep. Debbie Dingell with Reps. Clarke, Norton, Wilson, and Tlaib as original cosponsors.

The same day, it was referred to the Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary Committees; the action history shows no hearings, markups, or votes since.
The bill has 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to the sponsor.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill could still move, but no committee has scheduled any consideration of it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, covered employers, who face no new accommodation requirements because the bill has not advanced; the workers the bill would protect have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, so far; no new rules took effect

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 14, 2026, to create menopause accommodation rights mirroring the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act.

for.name: Reps. Yvette Clarke, Eleanor Holmes Norton, Frederica Wilson, and Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill has 7 Democratic cosponsors in total.

against.name: Chairs of the four committees of referral (Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary)
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: No committee has scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since its referral in July 2026.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a Democrat, and no Republican has signed on; no record of Republican opposition beyond inaction in committee.

industries.note: The bill would require these employers to provide accommodations, such as water access and rest breaks, and exposes them to damages and fees claims if they fail to. The bill's own findings argue the cost is offset by retaining experienced workers and reducing absenteeism, but the immediate compliance burden falls on employers. For workers, the employers' interest in avoiding accommodation requirements runs directly against the protections the bill creates.
These employers are exempt from the accommodation mandate, so the bill places no new requirements on them while their larger competitors absorb the compliance costs.

analysis.trajectory: A bill with 7 cosponsors that has sat in four committees since July, late in the second year of a session, very rarely reaches the floor on its own. Unless its provisions are attached to a larger package, it is likely to expire without a vote at the end of this Congress in January 2027.
